title: Group 17
objectives: Describe the colours and the trend in volatility of chlorine, bromine and iodine, and explain the trend in terms of intermolecular forces
Describe and explain the trend in bond strength of the halogen molecules and of the hydrogen halides
Describe the relative reactivity of the halogens as oxidising agents, including displacement reactions and reactions with hydrogen
Describe the relative thermal stabilities of the hydrogen halides
Describe the reactions of halide ions with aqueous silver ions followed by aqueous ammonia, and with concentrated sulfuric acid, and explain the trend in reducing power
Describe the reactions of chlorine with water and with cold and hot aqueous sodium hydroxide as disproportionation reactions, and the use of chlorine in water purification
why: The halogens are the clearest example of redox chemistry in action: chlorine bleaches and disinfects, bromine is used to test for alkenes, iodine to test for starch. Their trends link electronegativity, bond energy and intermolecular forces in one family, and halide tests with silver nitrate and sulfuric acid appear on almost every Paper 1 and practical paper.
intro: The Group 17 elements exist as diatomic molecules X₂. Each atom needs one electron to complete its outer shell, so the halogens are oxidising agents. This chapter covers their physical trends, their reactions as oxidising agents, the hydrogen halides, the reactions of halide ions, and the disproportionation reactions of chlorine.

blocks.h: Volatility decreases down the group: boiling points rise because the molecules have more electrons, so the instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces between them are stronger. Boiling never breaks the X–X bond.

The X–X bond gets weaker down the group: the atoms are larger, so the bonding pair is further from the two nuclei and is more shielded. The same applies to H–X bonds: H–Cl 431, H–Br 366, H–I 299 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.wrong: Iodine has a high melting point because the I–I bond is strong.
blocks.right: The I–I bond is the weakest. Iodine is a solid because of strong id-id forces between I₂ molecules.

blocks.q: Why does HI have a higher boiling point than HCl even though HCl is more polar?
o: HI has more electrons, so stronger id-id forces
blocks.why: The rise in id-id forces outweighs the fall in pd-pd forces.

sections.title: The halogens as oxidising agents; the hydrogen halides

blocks.h: A halogen oxidises by gaining electrons: X₂ + 2e⁻ → 2X⁻. Oxidising power decreases down the group because the atoms are larger and the incoming electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded.

A halogen oxidises the halide ions of any halogen below it: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂ (orange); Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂ (brown); Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂. Bromine cannot oxidise Cl⁻, and iodine cannot oxidise Br⁻ or Cl⁻.

blocks.name: halolab
blocks.title: Halogen test-tube lab
blocks.h: Mix halogen water with halide solutions to see which combinations react, or test each halide with silver nitrate and ammonia.

blocks.cap: H₂ + X₂ → 2HX: reactivity falls down the group
head: halogen
reaction with hydrogen
rows: reacts on heating with a catalyst
slow, incomplete and reversible even when heated (purple colour remains)

blocks.h: Thermal stability of the hydrogen halides

HCl is very stable; HBr decomposes slightly when strongly heated; HI decomposes easily (a hot wire in HI gives violet fumes of I₂). Stability decreases down the group because the H–X bond gets weaker (longer bond, larger atom).
Down Group 17: oxidising power of X₂ decreases; reducing power of X⁻ (and HX) increases; thermal stability of HX decreases.

blocks.cap: Test: add dilute HNO₃, then AgNO₃(aq), then NH₃(aq)
head: halide
precipitate
dilute NH₃(aq)
concentrated NH₃(aq)

blocks.h: Ag⁺(aq) + X⁻(aq) → AgX(s). Ammonia dissolves a silver halide by forming the complex ion [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺. Solubility in ammonia falls from AgCl to AgI. Dilute nitric acid is added first to remove carbonate ions, which would also give a precipitate.
All halides first react as bases: NaX + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HX. Then bromide and iodide, being stronger reducing agents, reduce the sulfuric acid.

blocks.name: h2so4
blocks.title: Halides with concentrated sulfuric acid
blocks.h: Choose a sodium halide to see the equations, the observations and how far the sulfur is reduced.
Reducing power of the halide ions increases from Cl⁻ to I⁻: the larger the ion, the further its outer electrons are from the nucleus, so the more easily they are lost.

blocks.q: Match each observation with NaI + concentrated H₂SO₄ to the species responsible:

blocks.h: In water treatment the active species is chloric(I) acid, HClO (and ClO⁻), which kills bacteria. In each reaction chlorine is both oxidised and reduced: a disproportionation.

blocks.q: What mass of NaClO₃ (M<sub>r</sub> 106.5) is formed when 0.300 mol of Cl₂ reacts with an excess of hot concentrated NaOH?
blocks.err: Assuming 1 mol Cl₂ gives 1 mol NaClO₃.

items: Cold gives NaClO (chlorate(I)); hot gives NaClO₃.
In ICl, iodine has an oxidation number of +1.
Cl is more electronegative and takes −1.

summary: Cl₂ pale green gas; Br₂ red-brown liquid; I₂ grey-black solid, purple vapour.
Volatility decreases down the group: more electrons, stronger id-id forces.
X–X and H–X bonds get weaker down the group (larger atoms).
Oxidising power of X₂ decreases down; a halogen displaces halides below it.
H₂ + Cl₂ explosive in light; H₂ + I₂ slow and reversible.
Thermal stability of HX decreases from HCl to HI; reducing power of X⁻ increases.
AgCl white (dilute NH₃ dissolves); AgBr cream (concentrated NH₃); AgI yellow (insoluble).
Concentrated H₂SO₄: NaCl → HCl only; NaBr → HBr, Br₂, SO₂; NaI → HI, I₂, SO₂, S, H₂S.
Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO (water treatment). Cold NaOH → NaCl + NaClO; hot NaOH → NaCl + NaClO₃. All are disproportionations.

flash.q: Colour and state of bromine at room temperature?
Why does volatility decrease down Group 17?
flash.a: More electrons, so stronger id-id forces between molecules

flash.q: Which X–X bond is strongest of Cl, Br, I?
Trend in oxidising power down Group 17?
Ionic equation: chlorine with bromide ions?
Does iodine react with bromide ions?
flash.a: No: iodine is the weaker oxidising agent

flash.q: Which silver halide is insoluble in concentrated ammonia?
Lowest oxidation state of S formed with NaI + H₂SO₄?
Why is I⁻ the strongest reducing halide?
flash.a: Largest ion: outer electrons furthest from nucleus and most shielded

flash.q: Why add dilute HNO₃ before AgNO₃ in the halide test?
flash.a: To remove carbonate ions, which also give a precipitate

practice.q: Predict, with a reason, whether bromine will react with aqueous potassium iodide. Give the ionic equation if it does.
practice.a: Yes: bromine is a stronger oxidising agent than iodine. Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂ (solution turns brown).

practice.q: Explain why HI is a stronger reducing agent than HCl.
practice.a: The I⁻ ion is larger, its outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are lost more easily (and the H–I bond is weaker).

practice.q: Describe how you would show that a solution contains bromide ions, giving all observations.
practice.a: Add dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃(aq): cream precipitate. It does not dissolve in dilute NH₃ but dissolves in concentrated NH₃.

practice.q: Write the two equations for the reaction of solid NaBr with concentrated H₂SO₄ and give the change in oxidation number of S.
practice.a: NaBr + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HBr; 2HBr + H₂SO₄ → Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O. S: +6 → +4

practice.q: Astatine is below iodine. Predict its state, colour of its silver salt and the thermal stability of HAt.
practice.a: Black solid; AgAt even less soluble (dark yellow/orange); HAt very unstable (weakest H–X bond).

practice.q: Show by oxidation numbers that Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O is a disproportionation.
practice.a: Cl: 0 in Cl₂, −1 in NaCl (reduced) and +1 in NaClO (oxidised): one element both oxidised and reduced.

assessment.q: Which halogen is a liquid at room temperature?
Which is the strongest oxidising agent?
assessment.why: Oxidising power decreases down the group.

assessment.q: Colour of the precipitate with AgNO₃ and chloride ions?
Which hydrogen halide decomposes most easily on heating?
With concentrated H₂SO₄, which halide gives only an acid–base reaction?
assessment.why: Cl⁻ is too weak a reducing agent.

assessment.q: Which gas smells of rotten eggs in the NaI + H₂SO₄ reaction?
Oxidation number of Cl in NaClO₃?
Products of Cl₂ with cold dilute NaOH?
Why does the boiling point increase from Cl₂ to I₂?
assessment.why: Intermolecular forces increase with electron number.

assessment.q: Which silver halide dissolves in dilute ammonia?
Which species in chlorinated water kills bacteria?

assessment_s.q:
Three unlabelled solutions are NaCl(aq), NaBr(aq) and NaI(aq).
(a) Describe a test using silver nitrate and ammonia that identifies each. [3]
(b) Describe a second test using chlorine water and a non-polar solvent. [2]
(c) Explain the trend in the reducing power of the halide ions. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) add HNO₃ then AgNO₃: white (Cl⁻), cream (Br⁻), yellow (I⁻); white dissolves in dilute NH₃; cream only in concentrated NH₃; yellow does not dissolve
(b) add Cl₂(aq) and shake with cyclohexane: no change for NaCl; orange organic layer for NaBr (Br₂); violet layer for NaI (I₂)
(c) reducing power increases Cl⁻ < Br⁻ < I⁻: larger ions, outer electrons further from the nucleus and more shielded, lost more easily

assessment_s.q:
Chlorine is used to make bleach and to treat water.
(a) Write an equation for the reaction of chlorine with water. [1]
(b) Give the oxidation numbers of chlorine in each chlorine-containing species in (a) and name the type of reaction. [2]
(c) Write the equation for the reaction of chlorine with hot concentrated NaOH and calculate the mass of NaClO₃ formed from 7.10 g of chlorine. [3]
assessment_s.a:
(a) Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO
(b) Cl₂ 0; HCl −1; HClO +1; disproportionation
(c) 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O; n(Cl₂) = 0.100 mol; n(NaClO₃) = 0.0333 mol; mass = 0.0333 × 106.5 = 3.55 g

pp.skill: Explaining volatility of the halogens
pp.mis: Explaining by the X–X bond strength
pp.stem: Chlorine is a gas at room temperature but bromine is a liquid. Why?
opts: The Br–Br bond is stronger than the Cl–Cl bond.
Br₂ molecules have more electrons, so the id-id forces between them are stronger.
pp.exp: Boiling only separates the molecules. More electrons → larger instantaneous dipoles → stronger id-id (London) forces. The covalent bond inside each molecule is not broken (and Br–Br is actually weaker).

pp.skill: Forces overcome when a halogen boils
pp.mis: Thinking the X–X bond breaks
pp.stem: Which forces are overcome when liquid bromine boils?
opts: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces between Br₂ molecules
pp.exp: Br₂ is non-polar; only id-id forces act between the molecules. Br₂ molecules are still present in the vapour.

pp.skill: Which property increases from chlorine to iodine
pp.mis: Mixing up trends in bond energy and boiling point
pp.stem: Which property increases from chlorine to iodine?
pp.exp: Boiling point rises (more electrons). X–X and H–X bond energies and electronegativity all decrease down the group.

pp.skill: Boiling points of the hydrogen halides HCl to HI
pp.mis: Thinking polarity increases down the group
pp.stem: The boiling points of HCl, HBr and HI increase in that order. Which factor is mainly responsible?
opts: increasing number of electrons, so stronger id-id forces
increasing polarity of the H–X bond
pp.exp: The H–X bond gets less polar down the group (smaller electronegativity difference), so pd-pd forces weaken; the rise is due to stronger id-id forces from more electrons.

pp.skill: Linking several halogen properties
pp.mis: Linking a high boiling point with a strong X–X bond
pp.stem:
Three statements about chlorine, bromine and iodine:
1 Chlorine has the weakest id-id forces and forms the most thermally stable hydrogen halide.
2 Iodine has the highest boiling point and the weakest X–X bond.
3 Bromine oxidises chloride ions.
Which are correct?
pp.exp: 1: Cl₂ has fewest electrons; H–Cl (431 kJ mol⁻¹) is the strongest H–X bond. 2: I₂ boils highest; I–I (151) is the weakest X–X bond. 3: false: Br₂ is a weaker oxidising agent than Cl₂.

pp.skill: Strongest reducing agent among halogen species
pp.mis: Mixing up halogens and halide ions
pp.stem: Which is the strongest reducing agent?
pp.exp: Halide ions are the reducing agents (they give electrons). I⁻ is largest, so its outer electron is held least strongly and is lost most easily.

pp.skill: Roles in a displacement reaction
pp.mis: Calling the halide the oxidising agent
pp.stem: Cl₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + I₂(aq). Which row is correct?
opts: KI acts as a reducing agent; chlorine is reduced
KI acts as an oxidising agent; chlorine is reduced
KI acts as a reducing agent; chlorine is oxidised
KI acts as an oxidising agent; iodine is reduced
pp.exp: I⁻ (−1) → I₂ (0): oxidised, so KI is the reducing agent. Cl₂ (0) → Cl⁻ (−1): reduced (Cl₂ is the oxidising agent).

pp.skill: Using displacement results to rank halogens
pp.mis: Ranking by number of reactions without thinking about roles
pp.stem: P, Q and R are halogens. Aqueous P₂ reacts with Q⁻ and R⁻; Q₂ reacts with R⁻ only; R₂ reacts with neither P⁻ nor Q⁻. What is the order of the halide ions as reducing agents, weakest first?
pp.exp: P₂ is the strongest oxidising agent, R₂ the weakest. The halide of the strongest oxidising halogen is the weakest reducing agent, so P⁻ < Q⁻ < R⁻.

pp.skill: Predicting whether displacement happens
pp.mis: Expecting any halogen to displace any halide
pp.stem: What happens when bromine water is added to potassium chloride solution?
opts: Chloride ions are oxidised to chlorine.
Bromine is reduced to bromide ions.
No reaction occurs; the solution stays orange.
pp.exp: Bromine is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine, so it cannot oxidise Cl⁻.

pp.skill: Statements about halogens and halides
pp.mis: Thinking halogens form cations
pp.stem: A student predicts four results. Which prediction is right?
opts: F atoms lose electrons to become F⁻
Br⁻ reduces things more readily than I⁻
pp.exp: I₂ is a weaker oxidising agent than Br₂, so no reaction. AgCl is white; halogens gain electrons to form anions; I⁻ is the stronger reducing agent.

pp.skill: Identifying three solutions from mixing results
pp.mis: Not checking every pair
pp.stem: X, Y and Z are three aqueous solutions. X + Y: no reaction. X + Z: immediate reaction, solution darkens to brown. Y + Z: no reaction. What are X, Y and Z?
opts: X Br₂; Y KCl; Z KI
X KCl; Y Br₂; Z KI
X I₂; Y KCl; Z KBr
X Br₂; Y KI; Z KCl
pp.exp: Br₂ + KI → I₂ (brown); Br₂ + KCl: no reaction; KCl + KI: no reaction. In C, I₂ + KBr would not react; in D, Br₂ + KI (X + Y) would react.

pp.skill: Combining Group 2 and Group 17 trends
pp.mis: Reversing one trend
pp.stem: Calcium and strontium each form a chloride and a bromide. Which compound contains the Group 2 element with the larger atomic radius and the halogen with the weaker X–X bond?
pp.exp: Sr is larger than Ca. Br–Br (193 kJ mol⁻¹) is weaker than Cl–Cl (242 kJ mol⁻¹).

pp.skill: Trends in the hydrogen halides
pp.mis: Thinking stability increases with size
pp.stem: Which row describes the hydrogen halides from HCl to HI?
opts: H–X bond energy increases; reducing power increases
H–X bond energy decreases; reducing power increases
H–X bond energy decreases; reducing power decreases
H–X bond energy increases; reducing power decreases
pp.exp: Larger halogen atoms make longer, weaker H–X bonds, so HI is least thermally stable and most easily oxidised (the strongest reducing agent).

pp.skill: Statement and explanation about hydrogen halides
pp.mis: Matching a true fact with a wrong reason
pp.stem: A hot glass rod is plunged into samples of HCl(g) and HBr(g). HBr gives some brown fumes but HCl does not change. Which explanation is correct?
opts: Br⁻ is a weaker reducing agent than Cl⁻.
The H–Br bond is weaker than the H–Cl bond.
Bromine is more reactive than chlorine.
pp.exp: H–Br (366 kJ mol⁻¹) is weaker than H–Cl (431 kJ mol⁻¹), so HBr partly decomposes to H₂ and brown Br₂ on heating. Br⁻ is a stronger reducing agent; chlorine is more reactive.

pp.skill: Matching halogen properties with correct explanations
pp.mis: Explaining a physical property with bond strength
pp.stem: Which row gives a correct statement and a correct explanation?
opts: Bromine is a liquid at room temperature | the Br–Br bond is strong
HI decomposes more easily than HCl when heated | the H–I bond is weaker
Chlorine is more volatile than bromine | chlorine has stronger id-id forces
Iodide is a better reducing agent than chloride | iodine is more electronegative
pp.exp: H–I (299 kJ mol⁻¹) is much weaker than H–Cl (431 kJ mol⁻¹). The other explanations are wrong (A, C) or the reason is reversed (D).

pp.skill: Choosing a correct property–explanation pair
pp.mis: Mixing up atoms gaining and losing electrons
pp.stem: Which row is correct?
opts: Br₂ has a higher boiling point than Cl₂ | Br₂ has more electrons and stronger id-id forces
HCl decomposes more readily than HBr | Cl is more electronegative than Br
Cl₂ is a stronger oxidising agent than Br₂ | a Cl atom loses electrons more readily
AgI dissolves in concentrated NH₃ | AgI is the most soluble silver halide
pp.exp: B is false (HCl is more stable). In C, the fact is right but halogens act by gaining electrons. AgI is insoluble even in concentrated NH₃.

pp.skill: Reactions of hydrogen iodide
pp.mis: Expecting a white precipitate with silver nitrate
pp.stem: Which statement about hydrogen iodide is correct?
opts: It reduces concentrated sulfuric acid, producing some hydrogen sulfide.
It is more thermally stable than HCl.
It gives a white precipitate with aqueous silver nitrate.
It does not react with chlorine.
pp.exp: I⁻ is a strong reducing agent and can reduce S from +6 down to −2. HI is the least stable HX; AgI is yellow; Cl₂ oxidises HI to I₂.

pp.skill: Comparing the reducing power of HCl and HI
pp.mis: Calling the halide an oxidising agent
pp.stem: HCl(aq) and HI(aq) are each exposed to oxygen: 4HX + O₂ → 2X₂ + 2H₂O. Which statement is correct?
opts: HCl reacts more readily because Cl⁻ is a stronger reducing agent.
HI reacts more readily because I⁻ is a stronger reducing agent.
HI reacts more readily because I⁻ is a stronger oxidising agent.
Both react equally because O₂ is the oxidising agent in both.
pp.exp: I⁻ loses its electron more easily than Cl⁻, so HI(aq) is oxidised by air (solutions turn brown with I₂); HCl(aq) is not.

pp.skill: Change of oxidation number of sulfur with iodide
pp.mis: Stopping at SO₂
pp.stem: Sodium iodide is warmed with concentrated H₂SO₄ and hydrogen sulfide is produced. Which row is correct?
opts: S: +6 → +4; iodide is an oxidising agent
S: +6 → −2; iodide is a reducing agent
S: +4 → 0; iodide is a reducing agent
S: +6 → −2; iodide is an oxidising agent
pp.exp: In H₂S, sulfur is −2 (from +6 in H₂SO₄). I⁻ gives electrons to sulfur, so it is the reducing agent.

pp.skill: Which halide reduces H₂SO₄ only as far as SO₂
pp.mis: Forgetting that iodide goes further
pp.stem: A halide reacts with concentrated H₂SO₄. The sulfur-containing products include SO₂, but nothing with sulfur in a lower oxidation state. Which halide is it?
pp.exp: Cl⁻ does not reduce H₂SO₄ at all. Br⁻ reduces it to SO₂ (+4). I⁻ reduces it further, to S (0) and H₂S (−2).

pp.skill: Halides that undergo both acid–base and redox reactions
pp.mis: Including chloride
pp.stem:
Two equations show halide Q⁻ reacting with concentrated sulfuric acid.
1 H₂SO₄ + Q⁻ → HSO₄⁻ + HQ
2 H₂SO₄ + 2Q⁻ + 2H⁺ → SO₂ + Q₂ + 2H₂O
Which halides can Q⁻ be?
pp.exp: All halides do reaction 1 (acid–base). Only Br⁻ and I⁻ are strong enough reducing agents for reaction 2.

pp.skill: Combining sulfuric acid and volatility clues
pp.mis: Not using both clues
pp.stem: Solid NaX reacts with concentrated H₂SO₄; the products include sulfur with an oxidation number of −2. Halogen Y₂ is more volatile than X₂. Which row could be correct?
pp.exp: S at −2 (H₂S) → only iodide. Y₂ must be more volatile than I₂: Br₂ (or Cl₂). Astatine is less volatile; NaBr gives only SO₂.

pp.skill: Colour of the halogen released
pp.mis: Mixing up the colours of Br₂ and I₂ vapour
pp.stem: Concentrated H₂SO₄ is added to solid KX. The only sulfur-containing gas formed is SO₂, and the halogen X₂ is also released. What colour is X₂ vapour?
pp.exp: Reduction only to SO₂ → bromide; Br₂ vapour is orange-brown. (I₂ vapour is purple; Cl₂ is yellow-green.)

pp.skill: Deductions from reactions with sulfuric acid
pp.mis: Forgetting the silver halide colours
pp.stem: X and Y are sodium halides. With concentrated H₂SO₄, X gives SO₂ but no H₂S; Y gives H₂S. Which statement is correct?
opts: Aqueous X turns orange when chlorine water is added.
Aqueous Y gives a white precipitate with AgNO₃(aq).
The silver halide from X does not dissolve in concentrated NH₃(aq).
pp.exp: X is NaBr: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂ (orange). Y is NaI: AgI is yellow. AgBr dissolves in concentrated NH₃.

pp.skill: Silver halide colours and solubility in ammonia
pp.mis: Mixing up cream and yellow
pp.stem: Which row is correct?
opts: colour of AgI: yellow; least soluble in NH₃(aq): AgI
colour of AgI: cream; least soluble in NH₃(aq): AgCl
colour of AgI: yellow; least soluble in NH₃(aq): AgCl
colour of AgI: white; least soluble in NH₃(aq): AgI
pp.exp: AgCl white (dissolves in dilute NH₃); AgBr cream (dissolves in concentrated NH₃); AgI yellow (insoluble even in concentrated NH₃).

pp.skill: Dissolving a silver halide precipitate
pp.mis: Thinking dilute ammonia dissolves AgBr
pp.stem: Aqueous silver nitrate and potassium bromide are mixed, forming a precipitate. Which reagent dissolves the precipitate to give a colourless solution?
pp.exp: AgBr (cream) dissolves in concentrated NH₃ to form [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, but not in dilute NH₃.

pp.skill: Identifying a soluble halide from tests
pp.mis: Forgetting that Ba²⁺ gives a sulfate precipitate
pp.stem: Compound Q dissolves in water. Q(aq) gives no precipitate with dilute H₂SO₄. With AgNO₃(aq) it forms a precipitate that does not dissolve even in concentrated NH₃(aq). What could Q be?
pp.exp: No precipitate with H₂SO₄ rules out Ba²⁺ (BaSO₄). Insoluble in concentrated NH₃ → AgI, so iodide: MgI₂.

pp.skill: Observations in two linked halide experiments
pp.mis: Forgetting that the fumes contain bromine
pp.stem: Reaction 1: concentrated H₂SO₄ is added to KBr and the fumes are bubbled into KI(aq). Reaction 2: KBr(aq) is mixed with AgNO₃(aq), then concentrated NH₃(aq) is added in excess. What is the final observation in each?
pp.exp: 1: the fumes contain Br₂, which oxidises I⁻ to I₂ (brown). 2: cream AgBr forms, then dissolves in concentrated NH₃.

pp.skill: Oxidation numbers in chlorine’s reaction with hot alkali
pp.mis: Writing +1 for the hot reaction
pp.stem: Chlorine reacts with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide. How does the oxidation number of chlorine change?
pp.exp: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O: Cl goes to −1 (NaCl) and +5 (NaClO₃): disproportionation.

pp.skill: Products of chlorine with hot alkali
pp.mis: Mixing up hot and cold conditions
pp.stem: Which chlorine-containing anions form when chlorine is passed into hot concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide?
pp.exp: Hot: chloride and chlorate(V). (Cold dilute alkali gives chloride and chlorate(I), ClO⁻.)

pp.skill: Products of chlorine with water
pp.mis: Thinking chlorine water contains only Cl₂
pp.stem: Chlorine dissolves in water and partly reacts. Which chlorine-containing species are formed by the reaction?
pp.exp: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. Chloric(I) acid, HClO, is the species that kills bacteria in water treatment.

pp.skill: Conditions to form chlorine in the +1 state
pp.mis: Choosing hot alkali
pp.stem: A manufacturer wants a salt with chlorine at +1 (as in bleach). What should chlorine be passed into?
opts: sodium hydroxide solution at room temperature
pp.exp: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O at room temperature: NaClO contains Cl(+1). Hot alkali gives NaClO₃ (+5).

pp.skill: Comparing three reactions of chlorine
pp.mis: Forgetting that chloride forms each time
pp.stem: Chlorine reacts separately with water, cold NaOH(aq) and hot NaOH(aq). Which statement is correct?
opts: Chloride ions (or HCl) are formed in all three reactions.
pp.exp: Water: HCl + HClO; cold: NaCl + NaClO; hot: NaCl + NaClO₃. Each is a disproportionation that forms Cl⁻.

pp.skill: Statements comparing hot and cold alkali
pp.mis: Assigning chlorate(V) to the cold reaction
pp.stem:
Chlorine reacts with cold and with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide.
1 Both reactions are disproportionations.
2 The hot reaction forms chlorate(V) ions.
3 The cold reaction forms NaClO₃.
Which statements are correct?
pp.exp: Both reactions take Cl from 0 to −1 and to a positive state. Cold gives NaClO (+1); hot gives NaClO₃ (+5).

pp.skill: Balancing chlorine with hot alkali
pp.mis: Not using electrons to balance
pp.stem: u Cl₂ + v OH⁻ → w Cl⁻ + y ClO₃⁻ + z H₂O. What is the simplest ratio u : v?
pp.exp: 3Cl₂ + 6OH⁻ → 5Cl⁻ + ClO₃⁻ + 3H₂O: u : v = 3 : 6 = 1 : 2.

pp.skill: Mass of chlorate(V) from an amount of chlorine
pp.mis: Using a 1 : 1 ratio
pp.stem: 0.450 mol of Cl₂ reacts with an excess of hot aqueous KOH. What mass of KClO₃ (M<sub>r</sub> 122.6) forms?
pp.exp: 3Cl₂ + 6KOH → 5KCl + KClO₃ + 3H₂O. n(KClO₃) = 0.450/3 = 0.150 mol; mass = 0.150 × 122.6 = 18.4 g.

pp.skill: Oxidation numbers in an interhalogen compound
pp.mis: Giving iodine the negative value
pp.stem: Iodine monochloride, ICl, is made from iodine and chlorine. What is the oxidation number of iodine in ICl, and which atom carries the δ− charge?
pp.exp: Cl is more electronegative than I, so Cl takes −1 and I is +1; the bond is polar with Cl δ−.

pp.skill: Colours, volatility, displacement and halides with sulfuric acid
pp.stem: This question is about the halogens and their sodium salts.

parts.q: Give the colour and state at room temperature of chlorine, bromine and iodine.
ms: Cl₂ pale green-yellow gas; Br₂ red-brown liquid; I₂ grey-black solid

parts.q: State and explain the trend in volatility from chlorine to iodine.

so stronger id-id forces, needing more energy to overcome

parts.q: Chlorine water is added to aqueous sodium bromide. Write the ionic equation and state the role of chlorine.
ms: oxidising agent: it gains electrons (is reduced)

parts.q: Write the equation for the acid–base reaction of concentrated H₂SO₄ with solid NaCl.
Equal amounts of NaCl, NaBr and NaI are each warmed with concentrated H₂SO₄. Which gives the highest yield of hydrogen halide? Explain.
ms: Cl⁻/HCl is too weak a reducing agent to reduce H₂SO₄, so none of the HCl is used up; HBr and HI are partly oxidised

pp.skill: Halogens as oxidising agents, bond strengths and a Hess calculation
pp.stem: The halogens are oxidising agents.

parts.q: Explain how the halogens act as oxidising agents, and the trend in oxidising power down the group.
ms: each atom gains an electron (X₂ + 2e⁻ → 2X⁻), taking it from the species oxidised
oxidising power decreases down the group: larger atoms, extra electron further from the nucleus and more shielded

parts.q: Describe the reactions of hydrogen with chlorine and with iodine.
ms: H₂ + I₂: slow, reversible, only partial reaction on heating (purple colour remains)

parts.q: Explain why HBr is less thermally stable than HCl.
ms: the H–Br bond is longer and weaker than H–Cl (Br is larger), so less energy is needed to break it

parts.q: Bromine reacts with ammonia: 3Br₂(g) + 2NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 6HBr(g). ΔH<sub>f</sub>: NH₃(g) −46, HBr(g) −36 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔH for this reaction.

pp.skill: Water treatment and the reactions of halide ions
pp.stem: Chlorine is used to treat drinking water. Halide ions can be identified by their reactions.

parts.q: Write an equation for the reaction of chlorine with water, and state the role of the active species.
NaI is warmed with concentrated H₂SO₄. Suggest the identity of the species that causes each observation: a black solid; a yellow solid; a smell of bad eggs.
ms: black solid: I₂; yellow solid: S

parts.q: Identify the sodium halide that reacts with concentrated H₂SO₄ in an acid–base reaction only.
Describe what is seen when AgNO₃(aq) is added to NaBr(aq), followed by concentrated NH₃(aq).
ms: which dissolves in concentrated ammonia to give a colourless solution

pp.skill: Making bleach: disproportionation and a mass calculation
pp.stem: Household bleach contains sodium chlorate(I), NaClO, made from chlorine.

parts.q: Give the reagent and conditions used to make NaClO from chlorine, and write the equation.
Define disproportionation and show that this reaction is one.
ms: the same element in one species is both oxidised and reduced

parts.q: Calculate the maximum mass of NaClO (M<sub>r</sub> 74.5) that can be made from 0.200 mol of Cl₂.
